# A cubic inequality for every three-by-three column-stochastic matrix

This note proves a standalone matrix theorem. It imposes no source calibration,
no conditions on row sums, and no condition on the locations of row maxima.
The extremal reduction was derived independently by Slab; the two-zero-row
boundary calculation was supplied by the contributor and independently checked by Slab.
The final section applies the theorem to every interior point and every
balanced three-normal circuit on an ordinary triangle, including cuts that
contain two vertices. This is an ordinary planar theorem, not (OC).

## 1. Statement and elementary reformulation

Let X=(x_ij) be a nonnegative 3 by 3 matrix with every column sum equal to 1.
For a nonnegative row x=(x_1,x_2,x_3), put

    Q_j(x)=x_j(x_k+x_l)-x_k x_l,  {j,k,l}={1,2,3},
    F(x)=max_j Q_j(x),   phi(x)=sqrt(F(x)).

Since Q_j-Q_k=2x_l(x_j-x_k), a largest entry is always a maximizing index.
In particular, if a is a largest row entry and b,c are the other two, then

    F(x)=a(b+c)-bc=a^2-(a-b)(a-c).                       (1)

Thus 0<=F(x)<=a^2. Write F_i=F(X_i), phi_i=sqrt(F_i).

**Theorem.** Every such matrix satisfies

    F_1+F_2+F_3+2 sqrt(F_1 F_2 F_3) <= 1.              (2)

Equivalently, the symmetric matrix B having zero diagonal and cyclic
entries B_12=phi_1, B_23=phi_2, B_31=phi_3 has largest eigenvalue at most 1.
Indeed, if its largest eigenvalue is at most 1, I-B is positive semidefinite,
and its determinant is the difference between the two sides of (2).
Conversely, (2) gives all F_i<=1, so all principal minors of I-B are
nonnegative: the minors of order two are 1-F_i and its determinant is
1-sum F_i-2sqrt(product F_i). The principal-minor criterion gives I-B>=0.

## 2. A positive weighted maximum cannot have two positive rows

Fix strictly positive constants c_1,c_2,c_3. Suppose a column-stochastic
matrix locally maximizes

    L(X)=sum_i c_i phi(X_i).                            (3)

Then at most one of its rows is positive in all three positions.

To prove this, suppose rows r and s are both fully positive. Arbitrary
small transfers X_r -> X_r+t v, X_s -> X_s-t v preserve the column sums and
nonnegativity for either sign of t.

First neither row can have a tied maximum. For any maximizing index j,
Q_j is positive at this row, so g_j=sqrt(Q_j) is smooth near it and is
bounded above by phi, with equality at the row. Replacing phi by any such
smooth branch in either of these two rows therefore gives a smooth
function still having a local maximum at the matrix. Its first derivative
under every transfer vanishes, so the two weighted branch gradients agree.
If one row had tied maximizing entries j,k, selecting each in turn while
keeping the other row's branch fixed would force their gradients to agree.
But at x_j=x_k,

    grad g_j-grad g_k=(x_l/phi(x))(e_j-e_k) != 0,

because the remaining entry x_l is positive. This is impossible.

Let j,k now be the unique maximizing columns of rows r,s. Their weighted
gradients have a common value lambda in R^3. Every coordinate of lambda is
strictly positive: for a unique maximum at j, the three derivatives of Q_j
are x_k+x_l, x_j-x_l, x_j-x_k, all positive.

Choose a nonzero transfer v with lambda dot v=0 as follows.

* If j=k, set v_j=0, v_k'=lambda_l', v_l'=-lambda_k', where k',l' are
  the other two columns. Then Q_j(v)=lambda_k' lambda_l'>0.
* If j and k are distinct, set v_j=v_k=1 and
  v_l=-(lambda_j+lambda_k)/lambda_l in the remaining column.
  Then Q_j(v)=Q_k(v)=1.

The weighted first derivative in each row is zero separately. For a
homogeneous quadratic Q and a point with Q>0, if grad Q dot v=0, then

    d^2/dt^2 sqrt(Q(x+t v)) at t=0 = Q(v)/sqrt(Q(x)).

Consequently the sum of the two weighted second derivatives is strictly
positive. The other row is unchanged, and the unique branches remain
maximizing for sufficiently small t. This contradicts a local maximum and
proves the claim. Notice that other rows may contain zeros; no smoothness
of those unchanged rows is required.

## 3. The boundary lemma: two rows have a zero

Suppose two distinct rows each have at least one zero. We prove (2)
directly. The positions of the chosen zeros fall into two cases, after
permuting rows and columns. Both operations preserve (2).

### Chosen zeros in the same column

Write the columns as

    (0,0,1), (a,b,c), (p,q,r),

where a+b+c=p+q+r=1. Then

    F_1=ap, F_2=bq, F_3=c+r-cr <= 1,
    sum F_i=1-(aq+bp).

By arithmetic-geometric mean,

    aq+bp >= 2sqrt(abpq) >= 2sqrt(F_1 F_2 F_3),

which is (2). This includes additional zeros.

### Chosen zeros in different columns

Write

    X = [ 0  a  b ]
        [ c  0  e ]
        [ r  s  t ],

where a=1-s, c=1-r, and b+e=L=1-t. All variables lie in [0,1]. Thus
F_1=ab and F_2=ce. Define

    Z=(s+t-st)(r+t-rt)=(1-aL)(1-cL).

Each of the three possible row-three quadratics is at most Z. The three
exact differences are

    Z-[r(s+t)-st] = t(1-r)[t(1-s)+2s],
    Z-[s(r+t)-rt] = t(1-s)[t(1-r)+2r],
    Z-[t(r+s)-rs] = t^2(1-r)(1-s)+2rs(1-t).

They are nonnegative, hence 0<=F_3<=Z<=1. Set z=F_3 and

    M = [ a          sqrt(ac z) ]
        [ sqrt(ac z) c          ].

The matrix N=(1-z)I-LM is positive semidefinite. Its diagonal entries are
nonnegative because

    1-z >= 1-Z = L(a+c-acL) >= L max(a,c),

and its determinant is exactly

    det N=(1-z)[(1-aL)(1-cL)-z] >= 0.

If L>0, apply N>=0 to (sqrt(b),sqrt(e)), whose squared norm is L. Division
by L gives

    ab+ce+2sqrt(ac z b e) <= 1-z,

which is (2). If L=0, then b=e=0 and F_1=F_2=0, while F_3<=1, so the same
conclusion holds without division. No strict positivity was used.

## 4. Completion of the stochastic theorem

The column-stochastic matrices form a compact set. Their matrices B depend
continuously on X, as does the largest eigenvalue J(X), so J has a maximum.
Suppose its maximum were greater than 1, at X*. At least two of the phi_i
are positive, because with only one positive edge J=phi_i<=1 by (1).
Therefore the graph of B(X*) is connected.

There is a strictly positive unit eigenvector w for its largest eigenvalue.
For completeness, maximize the Rayleigh quotient on the unit sphere and
replace the vector by its coordinatewise absolute value. The quotient
cannot decrease, so a nonnegative maximizing eigenvector exists. If a
coordinate were zero, its eigenvector equation and nonnegative entries
would force all neighboring coordinates to be zero; connectedness would
force the entire vector to vanish. Hence every coordinate is positive.

Keep this w fixed. The Rayleigh quotient at another matrix is

    w^T B(X) w = 2w_1w_2 phi_1(X)
                 +2w_2w_3 phi_2(X)+2w_3w_1 phi_3(X).

It is at most J(X), which is at most J(X*), and equality holds at X*.
Thus X* globally maximizes a positive weighted sum of the form (3).
Section 2 shows that at least two of its rows have a zero. Section 3 then
gives J(X*)<=1, a contradiction. The theorem follows.

For example, X with zero diagonal and every off-diagonal entry 1/2 has
F_i=1/4 and equality in (2); the constant is attained.

## 5. Exact row minimization on a uniform triangle

Let Xi be uniform in the barycentric probability simplex of dimension two,
and for a nonnegative row x=(x_1,x_2,x_3) put

    G_x(c)=Pr(x dot Xi <= c),
    psi(x)=inf_{c>0, G_x(c)>0} c/sqrt(G_x(c)).

Then psi(x)=phi(x). To see this, order x<=y<=z. For distinct entries and
x<c<y, G(c)=(c-x)^2/[(y-x)(z-x)], so c/sqrt(G(c)) is decreasing, or constant
when x=0. For y<=c<=z,

    G(c)=1-(z-c)^2/[(z-x)(z-y)].

The minimum occurs at

    c*=x+y-xy/z,

which lies in [y,z]. Differentiating the displayed elementary expression
shows that the sign changes from decreasing to increasing there; also
G(c*)=c*/z. Its squared minimum is therefore

    zc*=z(x+y)-xy.

For c>=z the ratio is c and cannot be smaller. Repeated-entry cases follow
either from the same formulas on the nonempty interval or directly:
if y=z>0 the minimum is z; if x=y=0<z the infimum is 0 as c decreases to 0;
if x=0<y the lower interval has the constant value sqrt(yz); and a constant
row z gives psi=z, including z=0. These cases also prove the formula without
any interchange of infima and approximation limits.

## 6. Application to arbitrary cuts of an ordinary triangle

Let K be any nondegenerate planar triangle, y an interior point, and
v_1+v_2+v_3=0 a spanning triple of nonzero normals. Define the actual raw
cap areas and coarea sections

    q_i=|K intersect {v_i dot (x-y)>=0}|,
    sigma_i=H_1(K intersect {v_i dot (x-y)=0})/||v_i||,
    k=|K|, M=sum_i q_i/sigma_i,
    f_i=2 sqrt(k q_i)/(sigma_i M).

All q_i and sigma_i are positive. Then, without any condition on how many
vertices a cap contains,

    sum_i f_i^2+f_1 f_2 f_3 <= 4.                       (4)

Here are the normalization details. Let P_j be the vertices, lambda_j the
positive barycentric coordinates of y, t_ij=v_i dot(P_j-y), Q_i=q_i/k,
and S_i=sigma_i/k. Let R_ij be the fraction of the opposite edge captured
by cap i, measured in that edge's own length. The divergence theorem for
the vector field x-P_j on the clipped triangle gives

    R_ij=Q_i-t_ij S_i/2.                               (5)

This identity also holds when a cutting line passes through a vertex:
vertices have zero edge-length and area, and the clipped polygons obey the
same flux formula. In that case the cut face has zero flux if t_ij=0.
The flux through the opposite edge is twice the full triangle area times
its captured edge fraction; the cut-face flux is +t_ij sigma_i, since its
outward normal points toward the excluded side.

Set

    X_ij=R_ij/(S_i M), a_i=Q_i/(S_i M).

The entries are nonnegative. The sum over i of X_ij is 1, because
sum_i Q_i/S_i=M and sum_i t_ij=0. Also (5) gives

    t_ij=2M(a_i-X_ij),    sum_j lambda_j X_ij=a_i.

For uniform barycentric Xi, the i-th cap is exactly
X_i dot Xi<=a_i, so G_{X_i}(a_i)=Q_i. Moreover
G'_{X_i}(a_i)=2M S_i. This derivative exists even at a vertex level, since
an interior line's section length is continuous; it is the usual area
coarea derivative. Consequently

    a_i G'_{X_i}(a_i)=2Q_i.

The function sqrt(G_{X_i}) is concave on its projection interval by the
ordinary planar Brunn-Minkowski inequality for nested caps, and remains
concave after its constant continuation beyond the top endpoint. Its
supporting tangent at a_i therefore passes through the origin. For c>0
with G(c)>0 it gives sqrt(G(c))/c<=sqrt(Q_i)/a_i. Thus

    phi(X_i)=psi(X_i)=a_i/sqrt(Q_i),  f_i=2phi(X_i).

Applying (2) proves (4). This also yields each individual row inequality
f_i+(f_j+f_l)^2/4<=2 by the elementary implication of the positive
semidefinite three-cycle (or by maximizing f_j+f_l at fixed f_i).
No mixed-integer center, global gluing, or higher-dimensional analogue is
asserted here.
